In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. 

Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot.

Prop. 41 prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.

Prop. 42 prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax.

The state constitution dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. 

Allegations against healthcare union's leader

Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months. Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization.

Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative.

The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” designed to derail the billionaire tax. 

If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years.

gislative Analyst’s Office estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year.

The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42. Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax.

The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. 

From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42, the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state.

Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance.

Billionaire opponents spend heavily

Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. 

Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot.

Prop. 41 prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.

Prop. 42 prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax.

The state constitution dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. 

Allegations against healthcare union's leader

Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months. Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization.

Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative.

The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” designed to derail the billionaire tax. 

If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years.

Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/), but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. Proponents of the tax criticized his Prop. 42 endorsement as “in lock step with his billionaire backers.” “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors,” said Debru Carthan, vice president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in a statement. “He’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask a couple hundred billionaires to finally pay their fair share.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Newsom has not yet taken a position on Prop. 41, another Brin-backed, anti-billionaire tax measure that would nullify Prop. 40 by subjecting the tax revenues to certain state spending limits and audits, said spokesperson Izzy Gardon. The billionaire tax measure, funded by one healthcare union, would put 90% of the money it collects toward the state’s healthcare program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal (https://calmatters.org/tag/medi-cal/). Newsom, along with many other leading California Democrats and most Republicans, has vocally opposed the billionaire tax and tried to negotiate to keep it off the ballot. In general during his two terms as governor he has opposed state-level taxes on assets, out of concern the wealthy will leave the state and deprive the state of their income tax revenue. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) endorsed the billionaire tax and polling shows a slim majority of likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/) support it. In response to the billionaire tax, Newsom this summer announced a proposal to impose a national tax on the wealthy, including a minimum tax rate on anyone with a net worth of more than $100 million. He also wants to undo corporate tax cuts that President Donald Trump and Congress approved in 2017, boost inheritance taxes and close loopholes the wealthy use to borrow from unrealized capital gains without paying income taxes. Critics from the left have tried to use his Prop. 40 opposition against him. Last weekend as he rallied for the billionaire tax, Democratic California Rep. Ro Khanna, another possible 2028 presidential contender, said donor relations were the “only reason” for Newsom’s opposition. “You can’t be anti-Trump and then do the bidding of Trump donors,” Khanna said in a video (https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ASPHAwXMW5k) with progressive former congressional candidate Saikat Chakrabarti. Khanna pointed to Brin, who has never donated to Newsom but has had a relationship with the governor for years. Newsom and Brin attended each other’s weddings. The tech magnate has recently also turned rightward, courting Trump’s favor. Newsom announced his endorsement of Prop. 42 on Friday along with his positions on most of the 14 ballot measures Californians are deciding on. He endorsed most measures on the ballot, but opposes Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/); Proposition 43, a measure to make it more difficult (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-prop-43-election-2026/) to pass most local taxes; and Proposition 44, a health union-backed measure (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) to dictate how much money clinics serving low-income patients must spend on patient care. He hasn’t yet taken a position on Proposition 45, the business-backed measure that puts time limits on the environmental review (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) process for new developments. gislative Analyst’s Office estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year.

The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42. Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax.

The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. 

From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42, the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state.

Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance.

Billionaire opponents spend heavily

Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. 

Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot.

Prop. 41 prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.

Prop. 42 prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax.

The state constitution dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. 

Allegations against healthcare union's leader

Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months. Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization.

Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative.

The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” designed to derail the billionaire tax. 

If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years.

Not only has Gov. Gavin Newsom vocally opposed the proposed California billionaire tax, but he also wants to prevent the state from ever passing a wealth tax in the future. 

On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. 

But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.

If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.

# ‘Billionaire’s Tax’ Is Losing Support, New Poll Finds
A new poll suggests support for California’s proposed billionaire tax, Proposition 40, may be slipping.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets exceeding $1 billion, with revenue primarily directed toward health care.
...
According to the Public Policy Institute of California’s October 2026 statewide survey, support for Proposition 40 has fallen six percentage points since September, dropping below a majority.
The poll found that 42% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposition, down from 52% in September.
More than 60% of Democratic voters support the proposed tax, compared with just 20% of Republicans.
The measure also has greater support among younger voters ages 18 to 34 and lower-income voters earning less than $40,000 annually.
Propositions 41 and 42, which are backed by opponents of Proposition 40, also have support from slim majorities of voters.
Proposition 41 would require audits of programs funded by new special taxes and restrict the state from exempting new taxes from its existing spending limit.
Supporters say the measure would make government more accountable, while opponents argue it would undermine the billionaire tax.
According to the poll, 48% of voters support Proposition 41.

Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that after leading by 8 points last month, it is now polling at only 44%, a lead of just one percentage point.

# California’s Billionaire Tax Slips From 52% Support to 42%
California’s Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on all billionaires in the state if more than 50% of voters fill in the box for “yes” by Tuesday.
It’s going to be a close one and may not pass, based on the latest polling.
...
The more recent polling has shown it to be even closer, with a Public Policy Institute of California poll taken Oct. 16-22 showing just 46% saying they would vote yes and 52% voting no.
An even more recent poll by a different organization, the University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, taken Oct. 19-25, shows just 42% saying they’ll vote yes and 50% pledging to vote no.
...
Opponents of Prop 40 have successfully gotten two of their own propositions on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42, which are essentially poison pills that would negate Prop 40 if it does pass.
Prop 41 is also close, with a recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showing 49% for no and 48% for yes.
The same pollster has Prop 42 at 51% yes and 47% no.

Yes support for California's Props 40, 41 and 42 fell in all four likely-voter polls from September to October 2026, with Prop 42 ahead of the billionaire tax in both October surveys.
The Public Policy Institute of California's October survey, fielded October 16–22 among 1,728 adults with a likely-voter subgroup of 1,086 and a margin of error of ±3.8 points, found 46% of likely voters voting yes on Prop 40 and 52% no.

I'm noting that the latest Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and IGS (Oct 19–25), with no newer measure polls found, and that the ActiVote poll covers only the governor race. The key remaining detail is PPIC's party split: 81% of Republicans support it, versus 28% overall among Democrats, with moderates at 49%.

I'm checking the PPIC party breakdown: 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates support Prop 41, against just 28% of Democrats. Working through the sample shares, the 48% overall yes figure would need Democrats to make up a sizable share of likely voters, with independents leaning yes around 50–55%.

I'm weighing how the Democratic share of the electorate could shift the 48% yes figure: high Democratic enthusiasm might push Democrats past their share in PPIC's sample, which would tilt toward No, though PPIC's turnout weighting may already account for that.

I'm looking for evidence on how ballot measures that poll under 50% in late polls tend to fare, and I'm checking for a general pattern where initiatives lose support as a campaign goes on.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll from late September actually covered Prop 41, since one listing shows it at 49-36 while another suggests that poll was about the voter ID measure.

I'm checking the IVN article to see whether the IVC poll really covered Prop 41, since that would be a Yes-leaning outlier from late September. I'm also testing a guess that the four polls behind Daily Kos's 43.0% average are IGS in August, PPIC and IGS in September, and IVC, and that guess checks out arithmetically.

I'm confirming that the IVC poll's 49–36 result on Prop 41 fits Daily Kos's four-poll average, since the arithmetic checks out exactly. That makes it a late-September poll that leaned Yes, but the October polls since then show support slipping toward 48%.

I'm checking the IVN article directly to confirm whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result belongs to the voter ID measure, since the listing I saw put it under Prop 39 and not Prop 41.

I'm checking which measure the "trails in PPIC and IGS, but led in SurveyUSA and IVP" line refers to, since the Prop 40 numbers (SurveyUSA 44–43, IVP 40–38) fit that description better than Prop 39 does.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result is about the voter ID measure (Prop 39) rather than Prop 41, since the IVN article URL points that way. That would mean the Prop 40 numbers I'd tied to that description are a separate matter.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 49–36 result for Prop 41 is a separate survey from the Sept 23–Oct 2 poll on voter ID, since the Independent Voter Project's Oct 5 numbers on Prop 40 are a different measure again.

I'm weighing the IVC poll against the others: its late-September 49–36 Yes result on Prop 41 would be the most favorable to Yes, which makes it an outlier next to PPIC's September 51–44 and IGS's 37–33. Since it is older than the October polls, which show support slipping, I'll note it as the outlier it is.

I'm going to fetch the IVN article to check the Prop 41 numbers, since an October poll from the Independent Voter Project could change the picture. I'm also planning to search for a source on how ballot measures tend to lose support over the course of a campaign.

The most recent Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25); no newer proposition polls turned up. I'll check the one Sept poll that showed Yes ahead, to confirm which measure it covered, and look for a historical base rate.

SAN FRANCISCO – Most polls answer one question: if the election were held today, who would win? We asked a slightly different question: who are the undecided voters, and how will they vote?
Surveys like the one sponsored by the Public Policy Institute of California are built to measure where a race stands at a particular point in time. They do that job well, in part by asking nearly every respondent to pick a side. The Independent Voter Project survey is built to study the voters who have not picked a side, or who can still be persuaded. It reports them separately, then looks at who they are.
That matters because undecided voters are not a random slice of the electorate. Who is still undecided varies by each race and ballot question, and the makeup of that group best guides where a close contest is likely to land.
For example, Proposition 39, the voter ID measure, leads in our survey, 43 percent to 40 percent among likely voters, with 17 percent undecided. But the Republicans we surveyed have largely made up their minds, and the voters who haven't are mostly Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. If those voters break the way similar voters already have, Prop. 39 lands at about 50 percent, a coin flip, but if they follow the usual pattern of voters who are unsure about a ballot measure and vote no, it will fail.
The survey of 2,906 likely voters was conducted Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, 2026 in English and Spanish and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Details are in the methodology section at the end of this story. Six weeks before the June 2 primary, an IVP poll (https://ivn.us/tag/ivp-poll/)was the first published survey in the New York Times tracker (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-governor-election-polls-2026.html?ref=ivn.us) to show Xavier Becerra breaking away (https://ivn.us/breaking-xavier-becerra-bolts-into-first-place-in-ivn-california-governor-poll-2026-04-20/) from the Democratic field for governor. He finished first.
Where the contests stand among likely voters today; undecided voters are shown in gold. How the Analysis Works
For each contest, the survey separates voters into those who have decided, including those who lean one way, and those who have not. It then compares undecided voters with decided ones on party, which party they trust, age, turnout history, region, and answers to related questions, such as whether they support voter ID in principle.
A statistical model trained on decided voters estimates how undecided voters with the same characteristics would likely vote. The model correctly predicts decided voters' choices about 9 times in 10 in the governor's race and on Props. 39 and 40.
The result is not a prediction of what will happen. It estimates where each contest is likely to end up if nothing changes between now and Election Day. Campaigns, news, and turnout can all change that.
Where the Contests Are Likely to Land
Likely outcomes are shares of the two-way vote if nothing changes before Election Day. Decided voters today compared with the likely outcome and range for each contest. The undecided vote looks different in every contest. On Prop. 39, it is heavily Democratic. In the insurance commissioner race, it looks much like the electorate as a whole, because so few voters know either candidate.
Who is still undecided: the makeup of the undecided vote changes from contest to contest. Prop. 39: Who Is Left to Decide
Asked the Voter ID question in plain terms, 62 percent of voters support requiring a government-issued ID to vote, with a free ID card for anyone who asks. However, the measure itself is much closer. Its official title, written by the Attorney General's office, says it "Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification."
When read this title, Republicans support Prop. 39, 81 percent to 10 percent, and only 9 percent are undecided. Democrats oppose it 59 percent to 19 percent, and more than one in five are undecided.
Of the voters still undecided on Prop. 39, 61 percent are registered Democrats, 24 percent are independents and 15 percent are Republicans. More than half of these undecided voters say they trust the Democratic Party more than the Republican Party.
To pass, Prop. 39 needs about 4 in 10 of its undecided voters, and our model estimates it gets about 41 percent. That leaves almost no cushion, and voters who are unsure about a ballot measure often vote no.
In the second wave of the survey, undecided voters were asked which way they would lean if they had to choose. Eight in 10 still could not say.
Prop. 40: Undecided Voters Don't Know Enough Yet
The idea of a one-time tax on billionaires to fund health care splits voters 40 percent to 38 percent. Prop. 40 itself trails 38 percent to 42 percent after voters hear the Legislative Analyst's Office estimate that it would raise tens of billions of dollars but could cost up to $1 billion a year in income tax revenue if wealthy residents leave California.
Its undecided voters are a different group. They are about half Democrats, a quarter independents, and a quarter Republicans. Most of them are not sure about the idea of a wealth tax at all: 62 percent of Prop. 40's undecided voters were also still undecided when the tax was described in plain terms .
To pass, Prop. 40 would need about 6 in 10 of its undecided voters. The model estimates it gets about half. In this survey, that makes Prop. 40 a toss-up that leans toward "No." PPIC's September survey found Prop. 40 ahead, and the difference between the two polls comes largely from Democratic and Latino voters, who are more supportive of the measure in PPIC's survey than in the one conducted by IVP.
Prop. 41, which would require audits of new special taxes, and Prop. 42, which would block new taxes on the ownership of financial assets and personal property, both lead comfortably. Our questions described those measures in plain terms rather than using their ballot labels, so read the size of their leads with caution. Because Props. 40, 41 and 42 conflict, the one with the most yes votes takes effect.
Support for Props. 39 to 42 by party registration. Insurance Commissioner: Two Democrats, and Most Voters Have No Idea
The race for Insurance Commissioner between state Sen. Ben Allen and Jane Kim, both Democrats, is the most open contest on California's ballot this November.
In the IVP survey, half of respondents saw only the candidates' names, as they will see them on the ballot. When given this choice, nearly two-thirds had no opinion, and the horse race was within the margin of error.
The other half of the IVP survey respondents were told that the Democratic Socialists of America endorse Jane Kim and that Ben Allen is a mainstream Democrat. With that one bit of information, Allen leads Kim, 36 percent to 23 percent, and his likely share of the two-way vote rises to about 63 percent. Republicans and independents supply most of the movement toward Allen, while Democrats stayed nearly evenly divided.
The insurance commissioner’s race will turn on what voters learn about the differences between the two Democrats on the ballot and whether Republicans, who have no candidate of their own, actually fill in the line and vote for one of the Democrats. Shown only names, nearly one in four Republicans said they would skip voting in this race.
The Los Angeles mayor's race features the same kind of matchup in a city with far fewer Republican voters. A recent UC Berkeley poll (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/politics/nithya-raman-karen-bass-la-mayor-election-polls/3946109/?ref=ivn.us) shows the DSA-endorsed challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, leading Mayor Karen Bass, with a third of voters undecided.
Half of the respondents saw only names. Half were told that DSA endorses Kim and that Allen is a mainstream Democrat. Governor and the Down-Ballot Races
Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton 48 percent to 38 percent. Fifty-five percent of the undecided voters in our survey are Democrats, and the model estimates they will break about 2-to-1 Becerra’s way. Hilton would need about 9 in 10 undecided voters to win. If nothing changes, Becerra's likely share of the two-way vote is about 57 percent.
The races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state have even more undecided voters, about one in four, and the undecideds are the same makeup as in the race for governor. Democrats Fiona Ma and Shirley Weber are likely to win their elections with 57 and 59 percent, respectively, if nothing changes. Republicans Gloria Romero and Don Wagner would each need about 7 in 10 undecided voters to break in their favor to win.
Independents Are the Swing Within the Swing
Independent voters, those registered with No Party Preference, the American Independent Party, or another minor party, make up about a quarter of likely California voters. They make up a larger share of the undecided vote, close to a third, in the races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Independents are not one bloc. More lean toward Democrats than Republicans: 29 percent trust the Democratic Party more, compared with 24 percent who trust the Republican Party more, and each group votes much like the party it trusts.
The largest group, though, 40 percent of independent voters, trusts neither party, even when asked to choose.
Those voters are where the close contests are most open:
They lean slightly toward Hilton, 40 percent to 33 percent, with nearly one in five undecided.
They support Prop. 39, 49 percent to 32 percent. That is the one group outside the Republican base where the measure has real support.
They split on Prop. 40, 36 percent to 40 percent, with nearly a quarter undecided.
Nearly half are undecided in the insurance commissioner race even after hearing which candidate DSA endorses.
Taken together, independents split about evenly in the governor's race.
They are also the voters most likely to leave part of the ballot blank. Only 65 percent of independents say they will vote on every race and measure, compared with 78 percent of Democrats and 75 percent of Republicans.

The independents who remain undecided are not the same voters from one contest to the next. The survey asked every respondent which party they trust more if they had to choose, and the answer changes the picture race by race.
Undecided independents by the party they trust more, if they had to choose. Governor. Republican-leaning independents have almost all decided. Only 3 percent of undecided independents in the governor's race trust Republicans more. Seven in 10 trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds split almost evenly between Becerra and Hilton, but undecided independents are likely to break about 63 percent for Becerra. Hilton's independents are already counted. The remaining voters are not his natural base.
Secretary of State. Only 1 in 10 undecided independents trusts Republicans more, and they are likely to break about 63 percent for Weber, compared with 53 percent among decided independents. The lieutenant governor's race is the exception among the candidate races: its undecided independents split about evenly, just as the decided ones do.
Prop. 39. Only 15 percent of Prop. 39's undecided independents trust Republicans more than Democrats. (Overall, 25 percent of independents trust Republicans.) The rest of the undecideds lean Democratic or trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds support the measure 58 percent to 42 percent. Undecided independents are likely to split about evenly. More than 4 in 10 of them are not sure about voter ID even in principle.
Prop. 40. Undecided independents on this question lean Democratic, which makes them more likely to vote yes than the independents who have already made up their minds. In other words, the conservative-leaning independent voters have already taken a side.
Insurance commissioner. With only names to go on, the undecided independents look like independents as a whole, including Republican-leaning voters. Almost no one knows the candidates, so party trust has not sorted anyone yet. That is why the race moves so sharply once voters learn who DSA endorses.
Undecided independents are likely to break differently than independents who have already decided. The groups of undecided independents are small, from about 80 to 230 respondents depending on the contest, so these figures show direction more than precise size.

SAN FRANCISCO – Most polls answer one question: if the election were held today, who would win? We asked a slightly different question: who are the undecided voters, and how will they vote?
Surveys like the one sponsored by the Public Policy Institute of California are built to measure where a race stands at a particular point in time. They do that job well, in part by asking nearly every respondent to pick a side. The Independent Voter Project survey is built to study the voters who have not picked a side, or who can still be persuaded. It reports them separately, then looks at who they are.
That matters because undecided voters are not a random slice of the electorate. Who is still undecided varies by each race and ballot question, and the makeup of that group best guides where a close contest is likely to land.
For example, Proposition 39, the voter ID measure, leads in our survey, 43 percent to 40 percent among likely voters, with 17 percent undecided. But the Republicans we surveyed have largely made up their minds, and the voters who haven't are mostly Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. If those voters break the way similar voters already have, Prop. 39 lands at about 50 percent, a coin flip, but if they follow the usual pattern of voters who are unsure about a ballot measure and vote no, it will fail.
The survey of 2,906 likely voters was conducted Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, 2026 in English and Spanish and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Details are in the methodology section at the end of this story. I'm noting that the latest Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and IGS (Oct 19–25), with no newer measure polls found, and that the ActiVote poll covers only the governor race. The key remaining detail is PPIC's party split: 81% of Republicans support it, versus 28% overall among Democrats, with moderates at 49%.

I'm checking the PPIC party breakdown: 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates support Prop 41, against just 28% of Democrats. Working through the sample shares, the 48% overall yes figure would need Democrats to make up a sizable share of likely voters, with independents leaning yes around 50–55%.

I'm weighing how the Democratic share of the electorate could shift the 48% yes figure: high Democratic enthusiasm might push Democrats past their share in PPIC's sample, which would tilt toward No, though PPIC's turnout weighting may already account for that.

I'm looking for evidence on how ballot measures that poll under 50% in late polls tend to fare, and I'm checking for a general pattern where initiatives lose support as a campaign goes on.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll from late September actually covered Prop 41, since one listing shows it at 49-36 while another suggests that poll was about the voter ID measure.

I'm checking the IVN article to see whether the IVC poll really covered Prop 41, since that would be a Yes-leaning outlier from late September. I'm also testing a guess that the four polls behind Daily Kos's 43.0% average are IGS in August, PPIC and IGS in September, and IVC, and that guess checks out arithmetically.

I'm confirming that the IVC poll's 49–36 result on Prop 41 fits Daily Kos's four-poll average, since the arithmetic checks out exactly. That makes it a late-September poll that leaned Yes, but the October polls since then show support slipping toward 48%.

I'm checking the IVN article directly to confirm whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result belongs to the voter ID measure, since the listing I saw put it under Prop 39 and not Prop 41.

I'm checking which measure the "trails in PPIC and IGS, but led in SurveyUSA and IVP" line refers to, since the Prop 40 numbers (SurveyUSA 44–43, IVP 40–38) fit that description better than Prop 39 does.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result is about the voter ID measure (Prop 39) rather than Prop 41, since the IVN article URL points that way. That would mean the Prop 40 numbers I'd tied to that description are a separate matter.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 49–36 result for Prop 41 is a separate survey from the Sept 23–Oct 2 poll on voter ID, since the Independent Voter Project's Oct 5 numbers on Prop 40 are a different measure again.

I'm weighing the IVC poll against the others: its late-September 49–36 Yes result on Prop 41 would be the most favorable to Yes, which makes it an outlier next to PPIC's September 51–44 and IGS's 37–33. Since it is older than the October polls, which show support slipping, I'll note it as the outlier it is.

I'm going to fetch the IVN article to check the Prop 41 numbers, since an October poll from the Independent Voter Project could change the picture. I'm also planning to search for a source on how ballot measures tend to lose support over the course of a campaign.

content.text: The most recent Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25); no newer proposition polls turned up. I'll check the one Sept poll that showed Yes ahead, to confirm which measure it covered, and look for a historical base rate.

SAN FRANCISCO – Most polls answer one question: if the election were held today, who would win? We asked a slightly different question: who are the undecided voters, and how will they vote?
Surveys like the one sponsored by the Public Policy Institute of California are built to measure where a race stands at a particular point in time. They do that job well, in part by asking nearly every respondent to pick a side. The Independent Voter Project survey is built to study the voters who have not picked a side, or who can still be persuaded. It reports them separately, then looks at who they are.
That matters because undecided voters are not a random slice of the electorate. Who is still undecided varies by each race and ballot question, and the makeup of that group best guides where a close contest is likely to land.
For example, Proposition 39, the voter ID measure, leads in our survey, 43 percent to 40 percent among likely voters, with 17 percent undecided. But the Republicans we surveyed have largely made up their minds, and the voters who haven't are mostly Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. If those voters break the way similar voters already have, Prop. 39 lands at about 50 percent, a coin flip, but if they follow the usual pattern of voters who are unsure about a ballot measure and vote no, it will fail.
The survey of 2,906 likely voters was conducted Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, 2026 in English and Spanish and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Details are in the methodology section at the end of this story. Six weeks before the June 2 primary, an IVP poll (https://ivn.us/tag/ivp-poll/)was the first published survey in the New York Times tracker (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-governor-election-polls-2026.html?ref=ivn.us) to show Xavier Becerra breaking away (https://ivn.us/breaking-xavier-becerra-bolts-into-first-place-in-ivn-california-governor-poll-2026-04-20/) from the Democratic field for governor. He finished first.
Where the contests stand among likely voters today; undecided voters are shown in gold. How the Analysis Works
For each contest, the survey separates voters into those who have decided, including those who lean one way, and those who have not. It then compares undecided voters with decided ones on party, which party they trust, age, turnout history, region, and answers to related questions, such as whether they support voter ID in principle.
A statistical model trained on decided voters estimates how undecided voters with the same characteristics would likely vote. The model correctly predicts decided voters' choices about 9 times in 10 in the governor's race and on Props. 39 and 40.
The result is not a prediction of what will happen. It estimates where each contest is likely to end up if nothing changes between now and Election Day. Campaigns, news, and turnout can all change that.
Where the Contests Are Likely to Land
Likely outcomes are shares of the two-way vote if nothing changes before Election Day. Decided voters today compared with the likely outcome and range for each contest. The undecided vote looks different in every contest. On Prop. 39, it is heavily Democratic. In the insurance commissioner race, it looks much like the electorate as a whole, because so few voters know either candidate.
Who is still undecided: the makeup of the undecided vote changes from contest to contest. Prop. 39: Who Is Left to Decide
Asked the Voter ID question in plain terms, 62 percent of voters support requiring a government-issued ID to vote, with a free ID card for anyone who asks. However, the measure itself is much closer. Its official title, written by the Attorney General's office, says it "Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification."
When read this title, Republicans support Prop. 39, 81 percent to 10 percent, and only 9 percent are undecided. Democrats oppose it 59 percent to 19 percent, and more than one in five are undecided.
Of the voters still undecided on Prop. 39, 61 percent are registered Democrats, 24 percent are independents and 15 percent are Republicans. More than half of these undecided voters say they trust the Democratic Party more than the Republican Party.
To pass, Prop. 39 needs about 4 in 10 of its undecided voters, and our model estimates it gets about 41 percent. That leaves almost no cushion, and voters who are unsure about a ballot measure often vote no.
In the second wave of the survey, undecided voters were asked which way they would lean if they had to choose. Eight in 10 still could not say.
Prop. 40: Undecided Voters Don't Know Enough Yet
The idea of a one-time tax on billionaires to fund health care splits voters 40 percent to 38 percent. Prop. 40 itself trails 38 percent to 42 percent after voters hear the Legislative Analyst's Office estimate that it would raise tens of billions of dollars but could cost up to $1 billion a year in income tax revenue if wealthy residents leave California.
Its undecided voters are a different group. They are about half Democrats, a quarter independents, and a quarter Republicans. Most of them are not sure about the idea of a wealth tax at all: 62 percent of Prop. 40's undecided voters were also still undecided when the tax was described in plain terms .
To pass, Prop. 40 would need about 6 in 10 of its undecided voters. The model estimates it gets about half. In this survey, that makes Prop. 40 a toss-up that leans toward "No." PPIC's September survey found Prop. 40 ahead, and the difference between the two polls comes largely from Democratic and Latino voters, who are more supportive of the measure in PPIC's survey than in the one conducted by IVP.
Prop. 41, which would require audits of new special taxes, and Prop. 42, which would block new taxes on the ownership of financial assets and personal property, both lead comfortably. Our questions described those measures in plain terms rather than using their ballot labels, so read the size of their leads with caution. Because Props. 40, 41 and 42 conflict, the one with the most yes votes takes effect.
Support for Props. 39 to 42 by party registration. Insurance Commissioner: Two Democrats, and Most Voters Have No Idea
The race for Insurance Commissioner between state Sen. Ben Allen and Jane Kim, both Democrats, is the most open contest on California's ballot this November.
In the IVP survey, half of respondents saw only the candidates' names, as they will see them on the ballot. When given this choice, nearly two-thirds had no opinion, and the horse race was within the margin of error.
The other half of the IVP survey respondents were told that the Democratic Socialists of America endorse Jane Kim and that Ben Allen is a mainstream Democrat. With that one bit of information, Allen leads Kim, 36 percent to 23 percent, and his likely share of the two-way vote rises to about 63 percent. Republicans and independents supply most of the movement toward Allen, while Democrats stayed nearly evenly divided.
The insurance commissioner’s race will turn on what voters learn about the differences between the two Democrats on the ballot and whether Republicans, who have no candidate of their own, actually fill in the line and vote for one of the Democrats. Shown only names, nearly one in four Republicans said they would skip voting in this race.
The Los Angeles mayor's race features the same kind of matchup in a city with far fewer Republican voters. A recent UC Berkeley poll (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/politics/nithya-raman-karen-bass-la-mayor-election-polls/3946109/?ref=ivn.us) shows the DSA-endorsed challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, leading Mayor Karen Bass, with a third of voters undecided.
Half of the respondents saw only names. Half were told that DSA endorses Kim and that Allen is a mainstream Democrat. Governor and the Down-Ballot Races
Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton 48 percent to 38 percent. Fifty-five percent of the undecided voters in our survey are Democrats, and the model estimates they will break about 2-to-1 Becerra’s way. Hilton would need about 9 in 10 undecided voters to win. If nothing changes, Becerra's likely share of the two-way vote is about 57 percent.
The races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state have even more undecided voters, about one in four, and the undecideds are the same makeup as in the race for governor. Democrats Fiona Ma and Shirley Weber are likely to win their elections with 57 and 59 percent, respectively, if nothing changes. Republicans Gloria Romero and Don Wagner would each need about 7 in 10 undecided voters to break in their favor to win.
Independents Are the Swing Within the Swing
Independent voters, those registered with No Party Preference, the American Independent Party, or another minor party, make up about a quarter of likely California voters. They make up a larger share of the undecided vote, close to a third, in the races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Independents are not one bloc. More lean toward Democrats than Republicans: 29 percent trust the Democratic Party more, compared with 24 percent who trust the Republican Party more, and each group votes much like the party it trusts.
The largest group, though, 40 percent of independent voters, trusts neither party, even when asked to choose.
Those voters are where the close contests are most open:
They lean slightly toward Hilton, 40 percent to 33 percent, with nearly one in five undecided.
They support Prop. 39, 49 percent to 32 percent. That is the one group outside the Republican base where the measure has real support.
They split on Prop. 40, 36 percent to 40 percent, with nearly a quarter undecided.
Nearly half are undecided in the insurance commissioner race even after hearing which candidate DSA endorses.
Taken together, independents split about evenly in the governor's race.
They are also the voters most likely to leave part of the ballot blank. Only 65 percent of independents say they will vote on every race and measure, compared with 78 percent of Democrats and 75 percent of Republicans.
Which Independents Are Still Undecided
The independents who remain undecided are not the same voters from one contest to the next. The survey asked every respondent which party they trust more if they had to choose, and the answer changes the picture race by race.
Undecided independents by the party they trust more, if they had to choose. Governor. Republican-leaning independents have almost all decided. Only 3 percent of undecided independents in the governor's race trust Republicans more. Seven in 10 trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds split almost evenly between Becerra and Hilton, but undecided independents are likely to break about 63 percent for Becerra. Hilton's independents are already counted. The remaining voters are not his natural base.
Secretary of State. Only 1 in 10 undecided independents trusts Republicans more, and they are likely to break about 63 percent for Weber, compared with 53 percent among decided independents. The lieutenant governor's race is the exception among the candidate races: its undecided independents split about evenly, just as the decided ones do.
Prop. 39. Only 15 percent of Prop. 39's undecided independents trust Republicans more than Democrats. (Overall, 25 percent of independents trust Republicans.) The rest of the undecideds lean Democratic or trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds support the measure 58 percent to 42 percent. Undecided independents are likely to split about evenly. More than 4 in 10 of them are not sure about voter ID even in principle.
Prop. 40. Undecided independents on this question lean Democratic, which makes them more likely to vote yes than the independents who have already made up their minds. In other words, the conservative-leaning independent voters have already taken a side.
Insurance commissioner. With only names to go on, the undecided independents look like independents as a whole, including Republican-leaning voters. Almost no one knows the candidates, so party trust has not sorted anyone yet. That is why the race moves so sharply once voters learn who DSA endorses.
Undecided independents are likely to break differently than independents who have already decided. The groups of undecided independents are small, from about 80 to 230 respondents depending on the contest, so these figures show direction more than precise size.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters 2019 fact check for the base rate, which found that 71% of measures lost support as election day approached. I may also look at the NBER paper on campaign spending to gauge how much the spending edge matters.

Is that true? We ran the numbers. Updated Oct. 18, 2019 In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform (http://www.capradio.org/articles/2019/07/17/california-bail-industrys-latest-effort-to-stay-in-business-ask-voters-for-constitutional-protection/), rent control (https://calmatters.org/housing/2019/09/big-rent-hikes-illegal-in-california-heres-what-to-know/), school construction (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/school-bond-breaking-up-with-pge-trade-war-stephon-clark-and-rabbis/) funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal.
