Sign up for free Δ That’s based on a bit of conventional wisdom, widely held among the types of people who fixate on such things, that support for ballot measures always declines the closer you get to election day. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. ABSTRACT
The conventional view in the direct democracy literature is that spending against a measure is more
effective than spending in favor of a measure, but the empirical results underlying this conclusion
have been questioned by recent research. We argue that the conventional finding is driven by the endogenous
nature of campaign spending: initiative proponents spend more when their ballot measure is likely
to fail. We address this endogeneity by using an instrumental variables approach to analyze a comprehensive
dataset of ballot propositions in California from 1976 to 2004. We find that both support and opposition
spending on citizen initiatives have strong, statistically significant, and countervailing effects. We
confirm this finding by looking at time series data from early polling on a subset of these measures.
Both analyses show that spending in favor of citizen initiatives substantially increases their chances

To what extent does campaign spending shape the electoral fate of citizen initiatives? This
empirical question has important implications for the normative debate over the role of money in
direct democracy elections (Gerber 1999, Broder 2000, Matsusaka 2004). If groups with a
concentrated interest in public policy can use their organizational advantages to raise large
campaign war chests that translate into votes for the initiatives that they propose, direct democracy
may not simply amplify the “voice of the people” as its early advocates promised (see Grantham,
1983, Ellis 2002, Goebel 2002, Piott 2003). By contrast, if spending in favor of initiatives does
not increase their chances of passage, powerful interests will not gain an advantage through the
money that they can raise.
While this important question has generated much scholarship from political scientists,
economists, and legal scholars, two distinct streams of the literature have provided different
answers to it. A long series of works that treat campaign spending levels as exogenous created a
conventional wisdom that expenditures have asymmetric effects: Money spent in opposition to
ballot propositions (including both citizen initiatives and measures placed on the ballot by
legislatures) lowers their expected vote shares or chances of passage, while spending in favor of
them is drastically less effective (Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Mastro et al. 1980, Lowenstein
1982, Magleby 1984, Schockley 1980, 1985, Schmidt 1989, Ji 1998, and Bowler and Donovan
1998). A recent review of the literature reports that these studies found “that heavy spending
against a measure tended to lead to the measure’s defeat, whereas heavy spending in favor of a
measure had a minimal impact (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, p. 470).” Though only a few studies

have probed why spending might have this asymmetric effect1 or why ballot proponents spend so
much even if their money appears to be wasted,2 many have pointed to the reassuring normative
implications of this empirical finding. “Such studies imply a role for money in direct democracy
that cuts against popular stereotypes. … [T]he deep pockets of business groups do not allow them
to ‘buy’ favorable policy (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, pp. 471-2).” At the same time, the
asymmetric effect of campaign spending may enable such groups to defend a status quo policy
against an energetic challenge.
Another stream of scholarship (Zisk 1987, Gerber 1999, Garrett and Gerber 2001) has

proposition and its backers (Banducci 1998, Stratmann 2005, 2006), that the effects of pro and con

proponents and opponents of a ballot measure can win more votes when they spend more money
suggesting a different view of money and direct democracy. If a well-organized interest or
business group opens its deep pockets for a ballot campaign, it may indeed be able to buy support
for a favorable outcome. Balancing this worry is the assurance that groups seeking to defend
existing policy have no predetermined advantage in a campaign against those who wish to
overturn the status quo.

We seek to address this consequential controversy in the literature by analyzing a
comprehensive dataset of ballot propositions in California4 from 1976 through 2004 and applying

from other types of propositions, and addressing other estimation issues. We argue that the much

majorities, while proponents of measures with a wide appeal can spend less and still win.

begin by taking the traditional approach to estimating the effect of spending on ballot measures,
which produces the asymmetric finding. When we treat campaign spending as exogenous and
assume that it has constant returns, it appears that opposition campaigns hurt ballot measures
while spending in favor of them is wasted.
This puzzling asymmetry disappears, however, when we use more flexible econometric
techniques that allow for diminishing returns and consider how the concentration of costs and
benefits can determine financial support for a policy proposal (Lowi 1964, Stigler 1971, Peltzman

I. Reasons to Doubt the Conventional Wisdom
While earlier studies compared the effect of spending patterns on the success rates of ballot
measures through bivariate studies (Lee 1978, Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Lowenstein 1982,
Owens and Wade 1986), recent works use multivariate models to predict the fate of propositions
by the levels of spending for and against them, along with other control factors (Ji 1998, Bowler
and Donovan 1998, Gerber 1999). Table 1 presents the most basic multivariate approach with our
data. It reports the results of a probit model explaining the success or failure of 329 propositions
in California from 1976 to 2004. The coefficients on these variables can be given a causal
interpretation only if pro and con spending levels have been exogenously and randomly assigned
to propositions. We also include controls for the type of election, the type of proposition, the
presence of a competing initiative, the number of other measures on the ballot, and economic
conditions. We coded all dichotomous variables that could be posed as questions with a “1”
indicating an answer of “yes” and a “0” indicating “no.” We estimate robust standard errors, and
include year fixed effects to account for the possibility that fiscal or electoral conditions make one
year a good or bad time for all initiatives on the ballot.

The results in Table 1 parallel the conventional finding in the literature. Money spent
against a proposition has a negative and strongly significant effect on its chances of passage. An
additional $1 million in opposition spending leads to an estimated 4.1% decrease in the probability
that it will pass. By contrast, the impact of spending in favor of a ballot measure is substantively
minuscule and falls far short of statistical significance. This basic model, which follows the
approach of many previous studies, reproduces the puzzling conventional wisdom that support and
opposition spending have asymmetric effects on the outcomes of direct democracy elections.5
Instead of accepting this counterintuitive result, we explore the substantive methodological
assumptions upon which it rests. Relaxing each assumption has a clear econometric implication,
and we explore the consequences of these estimation choices later in our empirical findings
section. In this section, we focus on our conceptual objections to the basic model reported in
Table 1, providing data and referencing other works that support our critiques.
A first troubling feature of the basic model is that it treats every proposition that appears
on a ballot as the same type of phenomenon, ignoring key differences in the path that a proposal
took to reach the ballot. We wish to draw a distinction between measures put on the ballot by
legislatures (the three6 types of measures that are commonly referred to as “legislative
propositions”) and direct citizen “initiatives”. Legislative propositions are less controversial,
much less likely to inspire spending on either side, and more likely to win than initiatives qualified
by voters and interest groups. The reasons for this lie in the rules that govern access to the ballot
5 In addition to the works that have informed the conventional wisdom, another stream of research finds that neither

propositions.
6 “Legislative propositions” include constitutional amendments proposed by the legislature, legislative bonds, and
legislative proposals to alter statutes that have been put in place by the citizens through initiatives (Legislative
Analyst’s Office 2009).
6

process, it must win two-thirds votes in both the Senate and the Assembly. Neither party ever held
such a supermajority during our period of study, meaning that some level of bipartisan agreement
was necessary to send every one of these legislative propositions to the voters (National
Conference of State Legislatures 2002, State Net 2005). Because of this, the measures were often
ideas with broad support that did not generate intense controversy or massive campaign spending.
Initiatives, by contrast, need not reflect the views of a wide cross-section of California
officeholders or voters. What they require is the intense support of a group that is sufficiently well
organized and well funded to collect a large number of voter signatures in a short amount of time.
To qualify for the ballot, statutory initiatives must be signed by the number of registered voters
that equals 5% of the votes cast in the last gubernatorial race, while initiative constitutional
amendments must be backed by 8% of that total. With only 150 days to collect these names,
nearly all initiative authors pay signature gathering firms $1-3 per name to collect the requisite
number of valid names (Gerber et al. 2001, p. 10). If a group is willing to pay more than a million
dollars to put its idea on the ballot, rather than spending a smaller sum lobbying the legislature to
pass it, we can expect that its proposal is opposed by a majority of legislators in Sacramento
(Lowenstein 1982, Kousser and McCubbins 2005). We can also expect that these citizen-backed
initiatives are less likely to draw wide support in the electorate than their legislatively-proposed
counterparts.
A look at the ballot measures in our sample demonstrates the differences between
legislative propositions and initiatives. The 192 legislative propositions that reached the ballot
from 1976 to 2004 attracted an average of $478,406 spent in support of them and $220,273 spent
in opposition, in constant 1982-84 dollars. Much more money flowed into initiative campaigns.

worse at the polls than legislative propositions. In our sample, 43% of citizen-authored measures
passed, while 70% of the legislature’s proposals were accepted by voters. Because they are so
clearly different from each other, we argue that these two types of propositions should not be
combined into the same analysis. Doing so would bias the estimated effects of spending in favor
of ballot measures toward zero, since it includes a class of measures (legislative propositions) that
generate little support spending and have high chances of passage because of the policy proposals
that they contain. Separating them from the analysis of citizen initiatives is a first step toward
breaking the endogenous link between the nature of a proposition and the spending that it attracts,
and thus isolating the “treatment” effect of campaign expenditures.
Some previous works have made the same division of ballot measures that we propose.
While the more comprehensive multivariate analyses by Ji (1998), Gerber (1999), and Bowler and
Donovan (1998) include both initiatives and legislative propositions, many of the earlier bivariate
analyses such as Lowenstein (1982), Shockley (1985), Price (1988), Meyers (1988), and Schmidt
(1989) looked only at citizen-authored initiatives. Garret and Gerber (2001) study both types of
ballot measures but include a dummy variable indicating the type of proposition in their models.
Because it is the citizen initiative that most commentators are referring to when discussing the
impact of money on direct democracy, analyses of this class of propositions will be most relevant
to the normative debate. We focus only on initiatives in the rest of our analysis.7
7 Because they are also initiated by citizens, are often controversial, and frequently generate expensive campaigns, we

attempts to overturn laws passed by the legislature which qualify for the ballot in the same manner as initiatives.

Our second objection to the conventional approach is that it assumes that spending will

spent $66 million in support of Proposition 5 in 1998 (California Secretary of State, 1999) had
spent a $67th million on it, this would have given their initiative the same boost that the second

transformations of expenditures provide a better fit of the data.

For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Sign up for free Δ That’s based on a bit of conventional wisdom, widely held among the types of people who fixate on such things, that support for ballot measures always declines the closer you get to election day. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. ABSTRACT
The conventional view in the direct democracy literature is that spending against a measure is more
effective than spending in favor of a measure, but the empirical results underlying this conclusion
have been questioned by recent research. We argue that the conventional finding is driven by the endogenous
nature of campaign spending: initiative proponents spend more when their ballot measure is likely
to fail. We address this endogeneity by using an instrumental variables approach to analyze a comprehensive
dataset of ballot propositions in California from 1976 to 2004. We find that both support and opposition
spending on citizen initiatives have strong, statistically significant, and countervailing effects. We
confirm this finding by looking at time series data from early polling on a subset of these measures.
Both analyses show that spending in favor of citizen initiatives substantially increases their chances
of passage, just as opposition spending decreases this likelihood.

To what extent does campaign spending shape the electoral fate of citizen initiatives? This
empirical question has important implications for the normative debate over the role of money in
direct democracy elections (Gerber 1999, Broder 2000, Matsusaka 2004). If groups with a
concentrated interest in public policy can use their organizational advantages to raise large
campaign war chests that translate into votes for the initiatives that they propose, direct democracy
may not simply amplify the “voice of the people” as its early advocates promised (see Grantham,
1983, Ellis 2002, Goebel 2002, Piott 2003). By contrast, if spending in favor of initiatives does
not increase their chances of passage, powerful interests will not gain an advantage through the
money that they can raise.
While this important question has generated much scholarship from political scientists,
economists, and legal scholars, two distinct streams of the literature have provided different
answers to it. A long series of works that treat campaign spending levels as exogenous created a
conventional wisdom that expenditures have asymmetric effects: Money spent in opposition to
ballot propositions (including both citizen initiatives and measures placed on the ballot by
legislatures) lowers their expected vote shares or chances of passage, while spending in favor of
them is drastically less effective (Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Mastro et al. 1980, Lowenstein
1982, Magleby 1984, Schockley 1980, 1985, Schmidt 1989, Ji 1998, and Bowler and Donovan
1998). A recent review of the literature reports that these studies found “that heavy spending
against a measure tended to lead to the measure’s defeat, whereas heavy spending in favor of a
measure had a minimal impact (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, p. 470).” Though only a few studies
2
have probed why spending might have this asymmetric effect1 or why ballot proponents spend so
much even if their money appears to be wasted,2 many have pointed to the reassuring normative
implications of this empirical finding. “Such studies imply a role for money in direct democracy
that cuts against popular stereotypes. … [T]he deep pockets of business groups do not allow them
to ‘buy’ favorable policy (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, pp. 471-2).” At the same time, the
asymmetric effect of campaign spending may enable such groups to defend a status quo policy
against an energetic challenge.
Another stream of scholarship (Zisk 1987, Gerber 1999, Garrett and Gerber 2001) has
found, often by explicitly considering that spending levels are endogenous to the nature of a
proposition and its backers (Banducci 1998, Stratmann 2005, 2006), that the effects of pro and con
spending can be symmetric under certain political conditions.3 These works have found that both
proponents and opponents of a ballot measure can win more votes when they spend more money
suggesting a different view of money and direct democracy. If a well-organized interest or
business group opens its deep pockets for a ballot campaign, it may indeed be able to buy support
for a favorable outcome. Balancing this worry is the assurance that groups seeking to defend
existing policy have no predetermined advantage in a campaign against those who wish to
overturn the status quo.

comprehensive dataset of ballot propositions in California4 from 1976 through 2004 and applying

of spending in candidate elections, we highlight the critical importance of estimation choices. We
begin by taking the traditional approach to estimating the effect of spending on ballot measures,
which produces the asymmetric finding. When we treat campaign spending as exogenous and
assume that it has constant returns, it appears that opposition campaigns hurt ballot measures
while spending in favor of them is wasted.

While earlier studies compared the effect of spending patterns on the success rates of ballot
measures through bivariate studies (Lee 1978, Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Lowenstein 1982,
Owens and Wade 1986), recent works use multivariate models to predict the fate of propositions
by the levels of spending for and against them, along with other control factors (Ji 1998, Bowler

in California from 1976 to 2004. The coefficients on these variables can be given a causal

The results in Table 1 parallel the conventional finding in the literature. Money spent
against a proposition has a negative and strongly significant effect on its chances of passage. An
additional $1 million in opposition spending leads to an estimated 4.1% decrease in the probability

opposition spending have asymmetric effects on the outcomes of direct democracy elections.5

assumptions upon which it rests. Relaxing each assumption has a clear econometric implication,
and we explore the consequences of these estimation choices later in our empirical findings
section. In this section, we focus on our conceptual objections to the basic model reported in
Table 1, providing data and referencing other works that support our critiques.

on a ballot as the same type of phenomenon, ignoring key differences in the path that a proposal
took to reach the ballot. We wish to draw a distinction between measures put on the ballot by
legislatures (the three6 types of measures that are commonly referred to as “legislative
propositions”) and direct citizen “initiatives”. Legislative propositions are less controversial,
much less likely to inspire spending on either side, and more likely to win than initiatives qualified
by voters and interest groups. The reasons for this lie in the rules that govern access to the ballot

ABSTRACT
The conventional view in the direct democracy literature is that spending against a measure is more
effective than spending in favor of a measure, but the empirical results underlying this conclusion
have been questioned by recent research. We argue that the conventional finding is driven by the endogenous
nature of campaign spending: initiative proponents spend more when their ballot measure is likely
to fail. We address this endogeneity by using an instrumental variables approach to analyze a comprehensive
dataset of ballot propositions in California from 1976 to 2004. We find that both support and opposition
spending on citizen initiatives have strong, statistically significant, and countervailing effects. We
confirm this finding by looking at time series data from early polling on a subset of these measures.
Both analyses show that spending in favor of citizen initiatives substantially increases their chances
of passage, just as opposition spending decreases this likelihood.

To what extent does campaign spending shape the electoral fate of citizen initiatives? This
empirical question has important implications for the normative debate over the role of money in
direct democracy elections (Gerber 1999, Broder 2000, Matsusaka 2004). If groups with a
concentrated interest in public policy can use their organizational advantages to raise large
campaign war chests that translate into votes for the initiatives that they propose, direct democracy
may not simply amplify the “voice of the people” as its early advocates promised (see Grantham,
1983, Ellis 2002, Goebel 2002, Piott 2003). By contrast, if spending in favor of initiatives does
not increase their chances of passage, powerful interests will not gain an advantage through the
money that they can raise.
While this important question has generated much scholarship from political scientists,
economists, and legal scholars, two distinct streams of the literature have provided different
answers to it. A long series of works that treat campaign spending levels as exogenous created a
conventional wisdom that expenditures have asymmetric effects: Money spent in opposition to
ballot propositions (including both citizen initiatives and measures placed on the ballot by
legislatures) lowers their expected vote shares or chances of passage, while spending in favor of
them is drastically less effective (Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Mastro et al. 1980, Lowenstein
1982, Magleby 1984, Schockley 1980, 1985, Schmidt 1989, Ji 1998, and Bowler and Donovan
1998). A recent review of the literature reports that these studies found “that heavy spending
against a measure tended to lead to the measure’s defeat, whereas heavy spending in favor of a
measure had a minimal impact (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, p. 470).” Though only a few studies

much even if their money appears to be wasted,2 many have pointed to the reassuring normative
implications of this empirical finding. “Such studies imply a role for money in direct democracy
that cuts against popular stereotypes. … [T]he deep pockets of business groups do not allow them
to ‘buy’ favorable policy (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, pp. 471-2).” At the same time, the
asymmetric effect of campaign spending may enable such groups to defend a status quo policy
against an energetic challenge.

found, often by explicitly considering that spending levels are endogenous to the nature of a
proposition and its backers (Banducci 1998, Stratmann 2005, 2006), that the effects of pro and con
spending can be symmetric under certain political conditions.3 These works have found that both
proponents and opponents of a ballot measure can win more votes when they spend more money

I've got the base rates now: CalMatters' 2019 review of about 80 PPIC-polled measures since 1998 found that 71% lost support as election day approached. Support dropped roughly 7 points a month on average, and education and tax measures soured fastest. That's the comparison I need.

Prop 41 is a tax-related measure, so I want more detail on how it's been polling. I'll also check the NBER paper on campaign spending and citizen initiatives, which looks at whether opposition money lowers passage odds and how initiatives tend to lose support over time in California.

I'm looking at how much money the No side has put into Prop 41 specifically, since the Yes side has a large spending edge. I also see that the SEIU-UHW committee, which is listed under Yes on 40, is counted by the FPPC as opposing 41, so the opposition funding picture is more tangled than it first looks.

I'm weighing the Yes side's roughly $58M edge for Prop 41 against the idea that the No side's money drives outcomes more than the Yes side's. The NBER findings suggest opposition spending cuts passage odds, but support spending also helps, so the high Yes-side spending could still lift the measure's chances.

I'm weighing the poll-decay pattern against the fact that the Yes side's spending edge could still lift Prop 41 despite opposition money. I'm also noting a citizen-initiative base rate of roughly one in three passing, though I still need a source for that figure.

I'm checking how the IVP/IVC poll framed Prop 41, since it used plain-language descriptions instead of the ballot label, so its lead shouldn't be compared directly with the other numbers. The poll's 49–36 result for 41 matches the NYT listing for the late-September survey, which I want to confirm.

The IVP poll's Prop 41 result of 49% yes and 36% no is confirmed as the source for the late-September figure, and it used plain-language wording rather than the ballot label. The PPIC/IGS polls, by contrast, showed Yes at 48 and 38 using the official label, so the two sets of numbers aren't directly comparable. I'm also noting that the IVP found independents are the group most likely to leave measures blank, and a blank vote effectively counts as a no for the yes share.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters 2019 fact check for the base rate, which found that 71% of measures lost support as election day approached. I may also look at the NBER paper on campaign spending to gauge how much the spending edge matters.

content.text: The Independent Voter Project poll that showed Prop 41 ahead used plain-language descriptions, not the official ballot label, so it isn't directly comparable to PPIC or IGS. Next I'll read the CalMatters historical analysis and the academic study on spending effects.

For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. ABSTRACT
The conventional view in the direct democracy literature is that spending against a measure is more
effective than spending in favor of a measure, but the empirical results underlying this conclusion
have been questioned by recent research. We argue that the conventional finding is driven by the endogenous
nature of campaign spending: initiative proponents spend more when their ballot measure is likely
to fail. We address this endogeneity by using an instrumental variables approach to analyze a comprehensive
dataset of ballot propositions in California from 1976 to 2004. We find that both support and opposition
spending on citizen initiatives have strong, statistically significant, and countervailing effects. We
confirm this finding by looking at time series data from early polling on a subset of these measures.
Both analyses show that spending in favor of citizen initiatives substantially increases their chances
of passage, just as opposition spending decreases this likelihood.

To what extent does campaign spending shape the electoral fate of citizen initiatives? This
empirical question has important implications for the normative debate over the role of money in
direct democracy elections (Gerber 1999, Broder 2000, Matsusaka 2004). If groups with a
concentrated interest in public policy can use their organizational advantages to raise large
campaign war chests that translate into votes for the initiatives that they propose, direct democracy
may not simply amplify the “voice of the people” as its early advocates promised (see Grantham,
1983, Ellis 2002, Goebel 2002, Piott 2003). By contrast, if spending in favor of initiatives does
not increase their chances of passage, powerful interests will not gain an advantage through the
money that they can raise.
While this important question has generated much scholarship from political scientists,
economists, and legal scholars, two distinct streams of the literature have provided different
answers to it. A long series of works that treat campaign spending levels as exogenous created a
conventional wisdom that expenditures have asymmetric effects: Money spent in opposition to
ballot propositions (including both citizen initiatives and measures placed on the ballot by
legislatures) lowers their expected vote shares or chances of passage, while spending in favor of
them is drastically less effective (Allen 1979, Lydenberg 1979, Mastro et al. 1980, Lowenstein
1982, Magleby 1984, Schockley 1980, 1985, Schmidt 1989, Ji 1998, and Bowler and Donovan
1998). A recent review of the literature reports that these studies found “that heavy spending
against a measure tended to lead to the measure’s defeat, whereas heavy spending in favor of a
measure had a minimal impact (Lupia and Matsusaka 2004, p. 470).” Though only a few studies

I'm pulling the SOS money totals for Prop 41: about $58.4 million in reported contributions so far. Only the Yes committee is listed as a measure-specific committee, so the No side seems to be funded through broader committees rather than one tied to 41.

I'm noting that the Yes on 41 committee is the only one listed for the measure, while SEIU-UHW is named as the source behind the No side. Next I want to check the CalMatters campaign-finance page for Prop 41, which may show total outside spending for and against it.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm pulling together the money totals for Prop 41 from the CalMatters voter guide, which runs through October 30, 2026. Supporters have about $58.4M in proposition-committee money, mostly from Building a Better California, with no independent expenditures reported for the Yes side. On the opposition side I'm tallying about $34.5M, and I need to watch that the SEIU-UHW figure of $31.97M is actually a "Yes on 40" committee that I'm counting as opposing 41, along with labor groups.

The money picture is more lopsided on the Yes side, though the contributions aren't the same thing as money actually spent yet. The No side's $34.5M looks mostly like SEIU's effort aimed at Prop 40, with only some going toward 41 and 42. Still, the gap matters, so I'm weighing whether that advantage helps Yes even though the poll numbers already show where things stand.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's bigger war chest, about 1.7 to 1 over the No side, is enough to matter in the final stretch, given that its committee money is still contributions rather than spending. Its funding comes from wealthy backers while the No side leans on labor, which may be more effective with messaging. With no new polls and high undecided numbers, I'm considering whether last-week ad spending could slow the decline in support.

I'm weighing the official ballot label for Prop 41 and how both the PPIC and IGS polls used the same official wording. Based on the poll trend and the Yes side's larger funding, I'm estimating the chance it passes at roughly 25–35%, with a final Yes vote share around 46%, though last-minute spending could shift that.

I'm working out the chance Prop 41 passes from the poll numbers: a mean Yes share around 46 to 48 with a few points of spread gives roughly a 15 to 35 percent chance of crossing 50, so a No outcome looks more likely.

I'm trying to back out the Democratic share of the PPIC sample from the party-level support numbers: Republicans and independents lean Yes, while Democrats are around three in ten. Plugging rough figures for each group into the 48% total should show how much of the sample Democrats make up.

I'm checking the partisan breakdown against the PPIC topline: with Republicans and independents leaning Yes and Democrats around three in ten, the mix lands near 48 to 49 percent, which matches the reported number. Getting above 50 would take a shift in who turns out or how independents break, and the party math doesn't point that way.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the No side looks more likely to win. I also want to check whether the poll numbers could be understating Prop 41's chances, for example if voters who back it are less visible in the polls.

I'm thinking through how a voter who opposes the billionaire tax (Prop 40) might vote Yes on 41, and whether some Democrats might vote No on 41 to protect 40. The polls put Prop 41 near 48% yes, and the pro-40 and pro-41 camps look about equal in size. Since Prop 41 only matters if Prop 40 passes with more votes, I'm checking how the two measures interact.

I'm noting that even if Prop 41 passes, it only has real consequences if Prop 40 also passes, though that doesn't change whether 41 itself wins. Some voters may be casting No on 41 to protect 40 while others vote Yes to oppose 40, so the poll figure is what I should rely on. I'm also considering blank ballots on the measure, which would count as effectively No, and whether the undecided share in the IGS poll partly reflects those voters.

I'm thinking about checking prediction markets like Kalshi or Polymarket for Prop 40 and 41, since a market-implied probability for Prop 41 passing would be a useful data point. I'll search for those markets directly.

I'm pulling together the money totals for Prop 41 from the CalMatters voter guide, which runs through October 30, 2026. Supporters have about $58.4M in proposition-committee money, mostly from Building a Better California, with no independent expenditures reported for the Yes side. On the opposition side I'm tallying about $34.5M, and I need to watch that the SEIU-UHW figure of $31.97M is actually a "Yes on 40" committee that I'm counting as opposing 41, along with labor groups.

The money picture is more lopsided on the Yes side, though the contributions aren't the same thing as money actually spent yet. The No side's $34.5M looks mostly like SEIU's effort aimed at Prop 40, with only some going toward 41 and 42. Still, the gap matters, so I'm weighing whether that advantage helps Yes even though the poll numbers already show where things stand.

I'm weighing whether the Yes side's bigger war chest, about 1.7 to 1 over the No side, is enough to matter in the final stretch, given that its committee money is still contributions rather than spending. Its funding comes from wealthy backers while the No side leans on labor, which may be more effective with messaging. With no new polls and high undecided numbers, I'm considering whether last-week ad spending could slow the decline in support.

I'm weighing the official ballot label for Prop 41 and how both the PPIC and IGS polls used the same official wording. Based on the poll trend and the Yes side's larger funding, I'm estimating the chance it passes at roughly 25–35%, with a final Yes vote share around 46%, though last-minute spending could shift that.

I'm working out the chance Prop 41 passes from the poll numbers: a mean Yes share around 46 to 48 with a few points of spread gives roughly a 15 to 35 percent chance of crossing 50, so a No outcome looks more likely.

I'm trying to back out the Democratic share of the PPIC sample from the party-level support numbers: Republicans and independents lean Yes, while Democrats are around three in ten. Plugging rough figures for each group into the 48% total should show how much of the sample Democrats make up.

I'm checking the partisan breakdown against the PPIC topline: with Republicans and independents leaning Yes and Democrats around three in ten, the mix lands near 48 to 49 percent, which matches the reported number. Getting above 50 would take a shift in who turns out or how independents break, and the party math doesn't point that way.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the No side looks more likely to win. I also want to check whether the poll numbers could be understating Prop 41's chances, for example if voters who back it are less visible in the polls.

I'm thinking through how a voter who opposes the billionaire tax (Prop 40) might vote Yes on 41, and whether some Democrats might vote No on 41 to protect 40. The polls put Prop 41 near 48% yes, and the pro-40 and pro-41 camps look about equal in size. Since Prop 41 only matters if Prop 40 passes with more votes, I'm checking how the two measures interact.

I'm noting that even if Prop 41 passes, it only has real consequences if Prop 40 also passes, though that doesn't change whether 41 itself wins. Some voters may be casting No on 41 to protect 40 while others vote Yes to oppose 40, so the poll figure is what I should rely on. I'm also considering blank ballots on the measure, which would count as effectively No, and whether the undecided share in the IGS poll partly reflects those voters.

I'm thinking about checking prediction markets like Kalshi or Polymarket for Prop 40 and 41, since a market-implied probability for Prop 41 passing would be a useful data point. I'll search for those markets directly.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. I'm weighing the markets against the rest of the evidence: Kalshi at 43% and Polymarket at 59% on Prop 41, drifting down from the mid-50s in late October. The poll near-tie, with PPIC at 48 Yes to 49 No, leaves little room for undecided voters to decide it, so this looks like a coin flip with a slight lean to No.

I'm weighing the remaining points for Prop 41: Republicans and most independents back it, and an IVP plain-language poll had it ahead 49 to 36 in late September. The "requires audits" framing and the anti-tax appeal could also draw support, though the Democratic-leaning electorate and Prop 13 sentiment cut the other way.

I'm considering whether the voters who want to block Prop 40 would back Prop 41, but only if they understand how the two are linked. The PPIC numbers put 41 at 48 and 40 at 46, so the two sit close together, which suggests some anti-40 voters aren't making that connection.

I'm weighing the probability of Prop 41 passing at roughly 30 to 40%, which would make No the more likely outcome. I'm checking whether the question about which side wins even has a clear answer on these numbers, since the estimate sits close enough to a coin flip that the framing matters.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the No side looks more likely to win Prop 41. I'll check the Yahoo article's date and prices before finalizing, but the market and poll evidence already points that way.

I'm checking the date on that Yahoo piece, since the Kalshi and Polymarket prices seem to have moved at different times. Polymarket still sits near 59% while Kalshi has dropped to 43%, which leaves the average around 51%. That makes the market look close to a coin flip, though the thin liquidity makes me less sure of it.

I'm going to check the Yahoo article for its date and the Prop 41 numbers, since it may show what bettors expected at the time. Polymarket's 59% and Kalshi's 43% are thin, so I'll only weigh them lightly.

Housing and infrastructure

The Kalshi app is displayed on a smartphone. Bloomberg via Getty Images
State finances and elections
Proposition 2 — Rainy Day Fund: Raises deposit limits and the maximum cap for the state's reserve fund. Kalshi: 92% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 4 — Public campaign financing: Repeals the prohibition on public funding for election campaigns. Kalshi: 9% | Polymarket: 22%

Advertisement

Proposition 38 — Immunology research bonds: Authorizes $8.4 billion in state bonds for medical research facilities. Kalshi: 82% | Polymarket: 72%
Proposition 44 — Clinic spending: Requires community health clinics to direct at least 90% of revenue toward patient programs and services. Kalshi: 8% | Polymarket: 11%

I'm comparing the figures on this page, and they don't agree. The summary lists Prop 41 as the closest measure at 51% Yes, with Kalshi at 47¢ and Polymarket at 89¢, and the 89¢ looks like an error or a different market. The text also calls Props 41 and 42 close to a coin flip, and I still need to check that against the table further down.

Now I'm checking the Prop 41 row in the table: 51% average, with Kalshi at 43% and Polymarket at 59%. The average is consistent with those two numbers, which is a relief after the mismatch in the summary.

The second snapshot gives Prop 41 a different reading: Kalshi at 42% and Polymarket at 43%, averaging 43% and labeled "Lean fail." The current page shows Kalshi at 43% and Polymarket at 59%, averaging 51% as "Toss-up." The page itself warns that these markets are thin, so a single trade can swing them, which could explain the gap. Taken together, Prop 41 looks like roughly 43 to 51% to pass.

The earlier Yahoo piece put Prop 41 at roughly 54 to 59% on the markets in late October, so the odds have shifted toward a fail since then. Now they sit around 43 to 51%, which points to a near coin flip with a slight lean toward No. With markets this thin, though, I wouldn't put much weight on that lean.

I'm weighing the market's roughly 43 to 51% pass estimate against my own read of the polls, which points closer to 25 to 35%. The markets are thin, so I'm inclined to discount them somewhat, though the poll average also shows a modest lean toward No. Given all that, I'm settling on something like a 35 to 40% chance that Prop 41 passes.

I'm weighing the poll numbers here: the most recent surveys show No slightly ahead, and Yes has been slipping in both since September. Undecided voters in one of them could break toward No, so the trend points the same way as the markets.

I'm working through the factors that point toward a No outcome for Prop 41: voters who are unsure tend to default to No or leave the ballot blank, which counts against the measure, and that confusion is reflected in reports of blank votes on 41 and 42. The party picture also leans against it, with most Democrats opposed.

I'm weighing the markets against the rest of the evidence: Kalshi at 43% and Polymarket at 59% on Prop 41, drifting down from the mid-50s in late October. The poll near-tie, with PPIC at 48 Yes to 49 No, leaves little room for undecided voters to decide it, so this looks like a coin flip with a slight lean to No.

I'm weighing the remaining points for Prop 41: Republicans and most independents back it, and an IVP plain-language poll had it ahead 49 to 36 in late September. I'm weighing the probability of Prop 41 passing at roughly 30 to 40%, which would make No the more likely outcome. I'm checking whether the question about which side wins even has a clear answer on these numbers, since the estimate sits close enough to a coin flip that the framing matters.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the No side looks more likely to win Prop 41. I'll check the Yahoo article's date and prices before finalizing, but the market and poll evidence already points that way.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

# California's billionaire tax loses support as election nears, poll finds
Here's what Californians should know about the poll, which surveyed a sample of 1,728 California adult residents and included 1,086 likely voters between October 16 and October 22.
## Poll's findings on other ballot measures, including wealth tax countermeasures and Proposition 39
The survey also examined two wealth tax countermeasures on November's ballot meant to mitigate the effects of Proposition 40 if it passes.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exclude revenue from the state spending limit, while Proposition 42 would prohibit new personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes passed after January 2026.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

I'm noting that Proposition 41 is one of three linked measures, mostly funded by Building a Better California. The reported totals for the Yes on 41 committee don't match between sources, roughly $58.3 million in one and $103 million in another, so I'm trying to work out why.

I'm checking the $103 million figure, which one article ties to a committee backing Proposition 41, possibly the combined Building a Better California spending on 41 and 42. I'm also looking at the No on 41 side, where SEIU-UHW has given several million, and what the late polls show, including a PPIC and a Berkeley IGS survey that point in different directions.

I'm now weighing whether a SurveyUSA poll or analysts' predictions could settle whether Proposition 41 gets over 50% yes, since the late polls are mixed.

I'm considering whether the pattern of late polls below 50% fits the common California trend where initiatives lose support as the election nears, and I'm looking for a Field Poll or PPIC analysis that tests whether measures starting with majority backing usually fade by election day.

I'm weighing whether Prop 41 can clear 50% yes, given that the Yes side is polling under half and slipping, while the No side has more undecided voters likely to break its way. I'm also considering that the No campaign has much less money than the Yes side, but still has strong backing from SEIU-UHW, and I want a base rate for how California initiatives fare when the Yes side is in that position.

I'm weighing whether the No side's smaller budget matters against the usual pattern where voters default to No when they're unsure, and I want to check how much each committee has actually spent on Proposition 41.

I'm weighing the blank-ballot effect: with three confusing measures, some voters may skip Prop 41, and undecided votes effectively count against it. The September polls had it near 50%, but the late ones have it around 48% and 38%, so the trend is falling, which points toward failure.

I'm now checking whether the Chamber of Commerce and taxpayer groups backing Prop 41 are pushing the auditing angle, since that tends to poll well. I'm also noting the ballot label wording about audits for new special taxes, which might draw some yes votes, and I want to look at the IVC Media poll from late September and whether any later polls exist, including an Emerson or SurveyUSA result for late October.

I'm now checking whether any results for Proposition 41 have been posted yet. The live pages I saw showed no counted votes, so I'm searching for "Proposition 41 wins" or "defeated" and early-returns coverage to confirm.

Now I'm pulling together the Prop 41 money totals, poll summaries, and any base-rate research on how California initiatives tend to fare when support slips before election day.

I'm going to check the SOS quick guide for Proposition 41 to confirm the money totals, and look for the IVC poll and any SurveyUSA result on the measure.

Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. No

Pro
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it.
