Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days.
Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and
state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition,
the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of
these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind,
with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on
topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’
initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.
Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63%
to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the
Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six
percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic
about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1
(60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three
legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title
and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37
(65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and
Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and
support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at
least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least
“somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and
the economy as well as housing costs and availability as
the most important issues facing California today.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is
headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming
majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in
the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49
percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults
and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big
problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of
confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
3/40
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At
the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52
House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters
will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’
initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter
engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton
(R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led
Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (61% to 36%).
Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats
support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the
Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra
over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions
and threats to democratic values and norms as the most
important problems facing the nation today.
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think
the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and
expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next
12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President
Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action
against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is
working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for
Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
4/40
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the
November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the
gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey), the 2022 general
election (62% October 2022 survey), and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey). Today,
majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of
independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with
the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions
are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election
(22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following
news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten
were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (25% very,
35% fairly) and in October 2018 (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69%
Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters
(65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were
similar in September (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (64%
Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more
Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most
independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to
37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic
candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
5/40
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are
more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half
or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an
“enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and
between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-
one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, shortly before the
June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024, ahead of the last congressional
election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more
enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature
placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say
they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds
for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey, 55 percent said
they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan
groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54%
to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition
1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on
this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014;
38 percent would vote no. In the September survey, 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent
would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23%
Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age,
gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns). Forty-five percent of
likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local
governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the
6/40
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose
one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2%
Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’
initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting
Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax).
There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents)
and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey, the
share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
September survey, 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for
Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and
declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in
the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters
say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies
be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September
survey, 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition
5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50
percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services). Forty-two
percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which
increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55
percent would vote no. In the September survey, 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would
vote no. Today, support for Proposition 43 varies across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans,
41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50
percent across regions.
7/40
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming
majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the
California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%)
8/40
or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the
state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make
temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely
voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September
2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most
Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters
(69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though
Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion
in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5
million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September
(61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are
more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote
yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology
Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would
vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans
are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and
demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits
Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail
ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the
envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were
similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats
9/40
would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic
groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma,
who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with
assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim
majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes,
compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger
(70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the
most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State
Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues
from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes
(48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and
independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across
demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal
Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other
than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and
independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across
demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health
Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit
community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less
than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no).
Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
10/40
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which
would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain
projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project
approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes,
while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support
vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
11/40
12/40
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living,
inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose
housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the
state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.

have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic
groups are pessimistic.

Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

14 propositions that could remake California taxes, housing, healthcare and elections (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)
In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

Californians and Their GovernmentOctober 2026
Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. gislative Analyst’s Office estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year.

The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42. Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax.

The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. 

From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents, attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42, the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state.

Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance.

Billionaire opponents spend heavily

Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. 

Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot.

Prop. 41 prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.

Prop. 42 prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax.

The state constitution dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. 

Allegations against healthcare union's leader

Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months. Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization.

Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative.

The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” designed to derail the billionaire tax. 

If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years.

On Friday he endorsed Proposition 42, a ballot measure that would cancel out Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/), the proposed billionaire tax. Prop. 42 would prohibit retroactive taxes like the one-time 5% tax on assets that would apply to any billionaire who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 if Prop. 40 passes. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property. That includes pensions and 401K accounts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) before retirees start drawing retirement income from them. It also includes other investments, financial assets, business holdings, art collections and all other forms of personal wealth that would be affected by the billionaire tax or any future wealth tax. Newsom’s decision to support Prop. 42 runs counter to his own Democratic Party and some labor unions. It also aligns him with some of the wealthy tech donors with whom he’s maintained longstanding relationships dating back to his days as mayor of San Francisco. Proponents primarily argue that middle-class workers’ retirements and pension accounts should never be taxed as assets before the gains are later taxed a second time as income, even though there is no such proposal (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/). Lawmakers have in the past proposed asset taxes but those bills went nowhere in the Legislature and any tax would require a two-thirds majority to pass. The proposed billionaire tax also exempts many kinds of retirement accounts. “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes so those savings are there when they need them,” Newsom said in a statement released by the proponents, who also include police and fire unions. But Prop. 42, funded and placed on the ballot by billionaire and Google co-founder Sergey Brin to defeat the billionaire tax, also would go further, by banning any new taxes on personal property.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the latest Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and IGS (Oct 19–25), with no newer measure polls found, and that the ActiVote poll covers only the governor race. The key remaining detail is PPIC's party split: 81% of Republicans support it, versus 28% overall among Democrats, with moderates at 49%.

I'm checking the PPIC party breakdown: 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates support Prop 41, against just 28% of Democrats. Working through the sample shares, the 48% overall yes figure would need Democrats to make up a sizable share of likely voters, with independents leaning yes around 50–55%.

I'm weighing how the Democratic share of the electorate could shift the 48% yes figure: high Democratic enthusiasm might push Democrats past their share in PPIC's sample, which would tilt toward No, though PPIC's turnout weighting may already account for that.

I'm looking for evidence on how ballot measures that poll under 50% in late polls tend to fare, and I'm checking for a general pattern where initiatives lose support as a campaign goes on.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll from late September actually covered Prop 41, since one listing shows it at 49-36 while another suggests that poll was about the voter ID measure.

I'm checking the IVN article to see whether the IVC poll really covered Prop 41, since that would be a Yes-leaning outlier from late September. I'm also testing a guess that the four polls behind Daily Kos's 43.0% average are IGS in August, PPIC and IGS in September, and IVC, and that guess checks out arithmetically.

I'm confirming that the IVC poll's 49–36 result on Prop 41 fits Daily Kos's four-poll average, since the arithmetic checks out exactly. That makes it a late-September poll that leaned Yes, but the October polls since then show support slipping toward 48%.

I'm checking the IVN article directly to confirm whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result belongs to the voter ID measure, since the listing I saw put it under Prop 39 and not Prop 41.

I'm checking which measure the "trails in PPIC and IGS, but led in SurveyUSA and IVP" line refers to, since the Prop 40 numbers (SurveyUSA 44–43, IVP 40–38) fit that description better than Prop 39 does.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 43–40 result is about the voter ID measure (Prop 39) rather than Prop 41, since the IVN article URL points that way. That would mean the Prop 40 numbers I'd tied to that description are a separate matter.

I'm checking whether the IVC poll's 49–36 result for Prop 41 is a separate survey from the Sept 23–Oct 2 poll on voter ID, since the Independent Voter Project's Oct 5 numbers on Prop 40 are a different measure again.

I'm weighing the IVC poll against the others: its late-September 49–36 Yes result on Prop 41 would be the most favorable to Yes, which makes it an outlier next to PPIC's September 51–44 and IGS's 37–33. Since it is older than the October polls, which show support slipping, I'll note it as the outlier it is.

I'm going to fetch the IVN article to check the Prop 41 numbers, since an October poll from the Independent Voter Project could change the picture. I'm also planning to search for a source on how ballot measures tend to lose support over the course of a campaign.

content.text: The most recent Prop 41 polls are PPIC (Oct 16–22) and Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25); no newer proposition polls turned up. I'll check the one Sept poll that showed Yes ahead, to confirm which measure it covered, and look for a historical base rate.

SAN FRANCISCO – Most polls answer one question: if the election were held today, who would win? We asked a slightly different question: who are the undecided voters, and how will they vote?
Surveys like the one sponsored by the Public Policy Institute of California are built to measure where a race stands at a particular point in time. They do that job well, in part by asking nearly every respondent to pick a side. The Independent Voter Project survey is built to study the voters who have not picked a side, or who can still be persuaded. It reports them separately, then looks at who they are.
That matters because undecided voters are not a random slice of the electorate. Who is still undecided varies by each race and ballot question, and the makeup of that group best guides where a close contest is likely to land.
For example, Proposition 39, the voter ID measure, leads in our survey, 43 percent to 40 percent among likely voters, with 17 percent undecided. But the Republicans we surveyed have largely made up their minds, and the voters who haven't are mostly Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. If those voters break the way similar voters already have, Prop. 39 lands at about 50 percent, a coin flip, but if they follow the usual pattern of voters who are unsure about a ballot measure and vote no, it will fail.
The survey of 2,906 likely voters was conducted Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, 2026 in English and Spanish and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Details are in the methodology section at the end of this story. Six weeks before the June 2 primary, an IVP poll (https://ivn.us/tag/ivp-poll/)was the first published survey in the New York Times tracker (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-governor-election-polls-2026.html?ref=ivn.us) to show Xavier Becerra breaking away (https://ivn.us/breaking-xavier-becerra-bolts-into-first-place-in-ivn-california-governor-poll-2026-04-20/) from the Democratic field for governor. He finished first.
Where the contests stand among likely voters today; undecided voters are shown in gold. How the Analysis Works
For each contest, the survey separates voters into those who have decided, including those who lean one way, and those who have not. It then compares undecided voters with decided ones on party, which party they trust, age, turnout history, region, and answers to related questions, such as whether they support voter ID in principle.
A statistical model trained on decided voters estimates how undecided voters with the same characteristics would likely vote. The model correctly predicts decided voters' choices about 9 times in 10 in the governor's race and on Props. 39 and 40.
The result is not a prediction of what will happen. It estimates where each contest is likely to end up if nothing changes between now and Election Day. Campaigns, news, and turnout can all change that.
Where the Contests Are Likely to Land
Likely outcomes are shares of the two-way vote if nothing changes before Election Day. Decided voters today compared with the likely outcome and range for each contest. The undecided vote looks different in every contest. On Prop. 39, it is heavily Democratic. In the insurance commissioner race, it looks much like the electorate as a whole, because so few voters know either candidate.
Who is still undecided: the makeup of the undecided vote changes from contest to contest. Prop. 39: Who Is Left to Decide
Asked the Voter ID question in plain terms, 62 percent of voters support requiring a government-issued ID to vote, with a free ID card for anyone who asks. However, the measure itself is much closer. Its official title, written by the Attorney General's office, says it "Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification."
When read this title, Republicans support Prop. 39, 81 percent to 10 percent, and only 9 percent are undecided. Democrats oppose it 59 percent to 19 percent, and more than one in five are undecided.
Of the voters still undecided on Prop. 39, 61 percent are registered Democrats, 24 percent are independents and 15 percent are Republicans. More than half of these undecided voters say they trust the Democratic Party more than the Republican Party.
To pass, Prop. 39 needs about 4 in 10 of its undecided voters, and our model estimates it gets about 41 percent. That leaves almost no cushion, and voters who are unsure about a ballot measure often vote no.
In the second wave of the survey, undecided voters were asked which way they would lean if they had to choose. Eight in 10 still could not say.
Prop. 40: Undecided Voters Don't Know Enough Yet
The idea of a one-time tax on billionaires to fund health care splits voters 40 percent to 38 percent. Prop. 40 itself trails 38 percent to 42 percent after voters hear the Legislative Analyst's Office estimate that it would raise tens of billions of dollars but could cost up to $1 billion a year in income tax revenue if wealthy residents leave California.
Its undecided voters are a different group. They are about half Democrats, a quarter independents, and a quarter Republicans. Most of them are not sure about the idea of a wealth tax at all: 62 percent of Prop. 40's undecided voters were also still undecided when the tax was described in plain terms .
To pass, Prop. 40 would need about 6 in 10 of its undecided voters. The model estimates it gets about half. In this survey, that makes Prop. 40 a toss-up that leans toward "No." PPIC's September survey found Prop. 40 ahead, and the difference between the two polls comes largely from Democratic and Latino voters, who are more supportive of the measure in PPIC's survey than in the one conducted by IVP.
Prop. 41, which would require audits of new special taxes, and Prop. 42, which would block new taxes on the ownership of financial assets and personal property, both lead comfortably. Our questions described those measures in plain terms rather than using their ballot labels, so read the size of their leads with caution. Because Props. 40, 41 and 42 conflict, the one with the most yes votes takes effect.
Support for Props. 39 to 42 by party registration. Insurance Commissioner: Two Democrats, and Most Voters Have No Idea
The race for Insurance Commissioner between state Sen. Ben Allen and Jane Kim, both Democrats, is the most open contest on California's ballot this November.
In the IVP survey, half of respondents saw only the candidates' names, as they will see them on the ballot. When given this choice, nearly two-thirds had no opinion, and the horse race was within the margin of error.
The other half of the IVP survey respondents were told that the Democratic Socialists of America endorse Jane Kim and that Ben Allen is a mainstream Democrat. With that one bit of information, Allen leads Kim, 36 percent to 23 percent, and his likely share of the two-way vote rises to about 63 percent. Republicans and independents supply most of the movement toward Allen, while Democrats stayed nearly evenly divided.
The insurance commissioner’s race will turn on what voters learn about the differences between the two Democrats on the ballot and whether Republicans, who have no candidate of their own, actually fill in the line and vote for one of the Democrats. Shown only names, nearly one in four Republicans said they would skip voting in this race.
The Los Angeles mayor's race features the same kind of matchup in a city with far fewer Republican voters. A recent UC Berkeley poll (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/politics/nithya-raman-karen-bass-la-mayor-election-polls/3946109/?ref=ivn.us) shows the DSA-endorsed challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, leading Mayor Karen Bass, with a third of voters undecided.
Half of the respondents saw only names. Half were told that DSA endorses Kim and that Allen is a mainstream Democrat. Governor and the Down-Ballot Races
Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton 48 percent to 38 percent. Fifty-five percent of the undecided voters in our survey are Democrats, and the model estimates they will break about 2-to-1 Becerra’s way. Hilton would need about 9 in 10 undecided voters to win. If nothing changes, Becerra's likely share of the two-way vote is about 57 percent.
The races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state have even more undecided voters, about one in four, and the undecideds are the same makeup as in the race for governor. Democrats Fiona Ma and Shirley Weber are likely to win their elections with 57 and 59 percent, respectively, if nothing changes. Republicans Gloria Romero and Don Wagner would each need about 7 in 10 undecided voters to break in their favor to win.
Independents Are the Swing Within the Swing
Independent voters, those registered with No Party Preference, the American Independent Party, or another minor party, make up about a quarter of likely California voters. They make up a larger share of the undecided vote, close to a third, in the races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Independents are not one bloc. More lean toward Democrats than Republicans: 29 percent trust the Democratic Party more, compared with 24 percent who trust the Republican Party more, and each group votes much like the party it trusts.
The largest group, though, 40 percent of independent voters, trusts neither party, even when asked to choose.
Those voters are where the close contests are most open:
They lean slightly toward Hilton, 40 percent to 33 percent, with nearly one in five undecided.
They support Prop. 39, 49 percent to 32 percent. That is the one group outside the Republican base where the measure has real support.
They split on Prop. 40, 36 percent to 40 percent, with nearly a quarter undecided.
Nearly half are undecided in the insurance commissioner race even after hearing which candidate DSA endorses.
Taken together, independents split about evenly in the governor's race.
They are also the voters most likely to leave part of the ballot blank. Only 65 percent of independents say they will vote on every race and measure, compared with 78 percent of Democrats and 75 percent of Republicans.
Which Independents Are Still Undecided
The independents who remain undecided are not the same voters from one contest to the next. The survey asked every respondent which party they trust more if they had to choose, and the answer changes the picture race by race.
Undecided independents by the party they trust more, if they had to choose. Governor. Republican-leaning independents have almost all decided. Only 3 percent of undecided independents in the governor's race trust Republicans more. Seven in 10 trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds split almost evenly between Becerra and Hilton, but undecided independents are likely to break about 63 percent for Becerra. Hilton's independents are already counted. The remaining voters are not his natural base.
Secretary of State. Only 1 in 10 undecided independents trusts Republicans more, and they are likely to break about 63 percent for Weber, compared with 53 percent among decided independents. The lieutenant governor's race is the exception among the candidate races: its undecided independents split about evenly, just as the decided ones do.
Prop. 39. Only 15 percent of Prop. 39's undecided independents trust Republicans more than Democrats. (Overall, 25 percent of independents trust Republicans.) The rest of the undecideds lean Democratic or trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds support the measure 58 percent to 42 percent. Undecided independents are likely to split about evenly. More than 4 in 10 of them are not sure about voter ID even in principle.
Prop. 40. Undecided independents on this question lean Democratic, which makes them more likely to vote yes than the independents who have already made up their minds. In other words, the conservative-leaning independent voters have already taken a side.
Insurance commissioner. With only names to go on, the undecided independents look like independents as a whole, including Republican-leaning voters. Almost no one knows the candidates, so party trust has not sorted anyone yet. That is why the race moves so sharply once voters learn who DSA endorses.
Undecided independents are likely to break differently than independents who have already decided. The groups of undecided independents are small, from about 80 to 230 respondents depending on the contest, so these figures show direction more than precise size.

I also see that the SEIU-UHW committee, which is listed under Yes on 40, is counted by the FPPC as opposing 41, so the opposition funding picture is more tangled than it first looks.

I'm weighing the Yes side's roughly $58M edge for Prop 41 against the idea that the No side's money drives outcomes more than the Yes side's. The NBER findings suggest opposition spending cuts passage odds, but support spending also helps, so the high Yes-side spending could still lift the measure's chances.

I'm weighing the poll-decay pattern against the fact that the Yes side's spending edge could still lift Prop 41 despite opposition money. I'm also noting a citizen-initiative base rate of roughly one in three passing, though I still need a source for that figure.

I'm checking how the IVP/IVC poll framed Prop 41, since it used plain-language descriptions instead of the ballot label, so its lead shouldn't be compared directly with the other numbers. The poll's 49–36 result for 41 matches the NYT listing for the late-September survey, which I want to confirm.

The IVP poll's Prop 41 result of 49% yes and 36% no is confirmed as the source for the late-September figure, and it used plain-language wording rather than the ballot label. The PPIC/IGS polls, by contrast, showed Yes at 48 and 38 using the official label, so the two sets of numbers aren't directly comparable. I'm also noting that the IVP found independents are the group most likely to leave measures blank, and a blank vote effectively counts as a no for the yes share.

I'm going to pull up the CalMatters 2019 fact check for the base rate, which found that 71% of measures lost support as election day approached. I may also look at the NBER paper on campaign spending to gauge how much the spending edge matters.

content.text: The Independent Voter Project poll that showed Prop 41 ahead used plain-language descriptions, not the official ballot label, so it isn't directly comparable to PPIC or IGS. Next I'll read the CalMatters historical analysis and the academic study on spending effects.

Is that true? We ran the numbers. Updated Oct. 18, 2019 In 2020, California voters will be asked to weigh in on some of the most contentious and consequential issues facing the state — criminal justice reform (http://www.capradio.org/articles/2019/07/17/california-bail-industrys-latest-effort-to-stay-in-business-ask-voters-for-constitutional-protection/), rent control (https://calmatters.org/housing/2019/09/big-rent-hikes-illegal-in-california-heres-what-to-know/), school construction (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/school-bond-breaking-up-with-pge-trade-war-stephon-clark-and-rabbis/) funding and inequality. For those hoping to make sense of the deluge of political polls and they’re likely to see over the next year, consider this a handy user guide. A new CalMatters analysis of survey data from the Public Policy Institute of California found, if history is a guide, that voters and other poll watchers can expect a few things. Support generally sags. The public’s net support for ballot initiatives (that is, how much public support exceeds opposition) declined by an average of about 7 percentage points each month. An equivalent change would be an initiative polling with 53% in support to 47% against in October, but then narrowly losing in November. There are exceptions. While 71% of the measures analyzed became less popular as election day approached, voters warmed to the other 29%. It depends on the measure. Voters have been quicker to sour on measures that tinker with education policy and raise taxes, but more steady on bond measure and tax decreases. It also depends on the election. The biggest drop off in net support for a measure occurred during low-turnout, non-presidential years. Our number-crunching was motivated by a simple question: When is a good poll still bad news? For years, a fairly consistent majority of Californians polled by the institute has backed hiking property taxes on longtime commercial landowners. The concept, known in policy shorthand as “split roll (https://calmatters.org/economy/2018/09/california-proposition-13-approval-rating/),” would require businesses to pay property taxes based on the current market value of their buildings and land, rather than on the initial purchase price. In short, it would be a massive tax increase on business, raising billions for local school districts and governments. But that sizeable base of support appeared to take a hit earlier this month. An October poll (https://calmatters.org/blogs/california-election-2020/2019/10/surveys-poll-gavin-newsom-homelessness-housing-ppic/) found that only 47% of likely voters support the idea of nixing the tax benefit for businesses, compared to 45% who oppose the idea. The remaining 9% weren’t sure. On its face, that might not seem like such a bad thing for split roll supporters — public sector unions who would benefit from an extra $7 billion to 11 billion in estimated revenue (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2017-055) and other progressives. But according to many analysts and commentators, that 2% margin of support is actually awful news if you favor the November 2020 proposal. Sign up for free Δ That’s based on a bit of conventional wisdom, widely held among the types of people who fixate on such things, that support for ballot measures always declines the closer you get to election day. Since 1998, the institute has asked Californians it deems “likely voters” about 80 ballot measures. An examination of how opinion on each of those ballot measures has shifted over time—from polls as early as a year out from election day to the certified ballot box results themselves—shows that the conventional wisdom generally holds up. The vast majority of ballot measures analyzed saw a decline in public support as election day approached. There were exceptions and the range was enormous, but the average worked out to 6.6% percentage points per month. Why? The most common theory comes down to timing, said Dean Bonner, a survey director at the institute. A new policy proposal may sound good on paper. Then the attack ads and editorializing begins. “Wherever a ballot measure campaign starts off, it’s starting off without there being a ‘No’ campaign,” he said. A blog post from the California Chamber of Commerce gleefully made that point (https://calchamberalert.com/2019/10/04/poll-shows-dropping-support-for-split-roll-largest-tax-hike-in-history/) about the new survey on split roll, which it calls the “largest tax hike in history”: “Support for a split roll initiative has dipped below 50%, even before facing a serious opposition campaign — and without any mention in the survey question that the initiative would alter Proposition 13, a landmark law most voters typically associate with popular residential tax protections.” Lack of a counter campaign may help to explain why some measures fare better over time. In other words, money matters. A study of California initiatives between 1976 and 2004 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w16356)found that ballot campaigns where opposition more than doubled spending on the pro side lost public support twice as fast as ballot measures for which the opposite was true. “Support for each type of initiative declines over the course of the campaign, but if the supporting side has far deeper pockets than the opposition, that decline is far less sharp, leaving ballot measures with just enough support to often win,” Thad Kousser, one of the authors of the study, explained in an email. Take bond measures, for example, where average support has actually inched up slightly. While plenty of interests are willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there’s no huge anti-debt lobby. No surprise then that bonds also have a disproportionately good track record at the ballot box. While only 35% of the 80 ballot measures analyzed ended up passing, 82% of bond measures were approved. Support for bond measures, for example, tends to remain relatively steady through an election season. On average, support for these measures has actually inched up slightly. While there are plenty of interests willing to spend big in support of new financing for public infrastructure, with the exception of small government groups like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, there isn’t a huge anti-debt lobby. Another potential explanation why most ballot measures drift downward in the polls is the “cautious voter” theory. If voters aren’t sure about a big change to state law, the thinking goes, they’ll err on the side of caution and default to the ‘no.’ But without asking individual voters, it’s harder to say whether that actually happens. Ballot measures that elicited more shoulder shrugging in surveys prior to election day weren’t any more or less likely to see their support drop off — or to fail on election day. All this might seem ominous to split roll supporters, but they do have three reasons to hold out hope. First, ballot measure polls seem to overshoot the final election result the most during off-year elections. During midterm primary elections and other off-year contests, the typical measure saw a drop off in its net popularity by more than 10 percentage points. But in the run up to general election, particularly during presidential years, the decline was much more modest. Second: How a measure is described on the ballot probably matters. And the Attorney General this week gave the split roll campaign got a very favorable title, which emphasizes the new funding rather than the tax hike: “Increases Funding for Public Schools, Community Colleges, and Local Government Services by Changing Tax Assessment of Commercial and Industrial Property.” Third, there are exceptions to every rule. ABSTRACT
The conventional view in the direct democracy literature is that spending against a measure is more
effective than spending in favor of a measure, but the empirical results underlying this conclusion
have been questioned by recent research. We argue that the conventional finding is driven by the endogenous
nature of campaign spending: initiative proponents spend more when their ballot measure is likely
to fail. We address this endogeneity by using an instrumental variables approach to analyze a comprehensive
dataset of ballot propositions in California from 1976 to 2004. We find that both support and opposition
spending on citizen initiatives have strong, statistically significant, and countervailing effects. We
confirm this finding by looking at time series data from early polling on a subset of these measures.
Both analyses show that spending in favor of citizen initiatives substantially increases their chances
of passage, just as opposition spending decreases this likelihood.
